records.sourceFile: Cannabis, cannabidiol and tetrahydrocannabinol in sport - An overview.pdf

paper.citation: Kennedy M. Cannabis, cannabidiol and tetrahydrocannabinol in sport: an overview. Accepted manuscript. 2022.
paper.abstract: This narrative review states that the World Anti-Doping Agency permits CBD in competition but still bans THC and other cannabinoids. It concludes that CBD and THC do not enhance performance, that CBD's anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects have not been evaluated in sport, and that some CBD products contain THC and can cause a positive drug test.
paper.tldr: Cannabis use by athletes appears common but not universal, and the review finds no good evidence that CBD or THC improves performance. THC impaired aerobic performance in the studies cited, and the three small CBD trials in trained lifters and untrained men showed no clear benefit for muscle soreness or strength.
paper.methods: Narrative review. Literature was identified through PubMed, Medline, Google and the author's reprint collection. No systematic search or formal quality appraisal is described.
paper.findings: Acute THC reduced aerobic performance and possibly strength in the studies cited. Three CBD studies (23 trained lifters in three non-crossed groups, 16 trained lifters in a double-blind crossover, and 13 untrained men in a double-blind crossover) found no substantial effect on performance, with one reporting lower creatine kinase and myoglobin after CBD than placebo (p<0.05). In a survey of 517 UK rugby players, 133 had used CBD, most often for pain (80% of users) and sleep (78%).
paper.limitations: The review is non-systematic and the author states that controlled data on CBD in athletes are very limited. Adverse effect evidence in sport comes mainly from surveys and case reports. The PDF is an accepted manuscript and the journal, volume, pages and publication year are not printed in the text; the year 2022 comes from the Crossref record and is consistent with the text's reference to 'the position in 2022' and 2022 access dates.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should assume that THC is banned in competition and that some CBD products may contain enough THC to produce a positive test. Athletes who ask about CBD for recovery or sleep should be told that controlled evidence in athletes is lacking. The author advises older athletes and those with known cardiac conditions to be aware of the risk of arrhythmias and acute events, which in the cited reports were linked to THC.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not expect cannabinoids to enhance training or competition performance. THC was shown to impair aerobic performance in the cited studies, and CBD studies showed no clear effect on strength or muscle damage.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate return to sport. It notes CBD's potential for pain and inflammation without sport-specific trials, so it cannot support a clinical return-to-play decision about cannabinoids.

records.sourceFile: The effects of electronic nicotine delivery systems on athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Young SE, Henderson CA, Couperus KS. The Effects of Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems on Athletes. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(4):146-150.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers the rise of electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) and their effects on athletes, including cardiovascular, pulmonary and recovery outcomes. It also describes vaping-associated lung injury and its presenting features. The authors conclude that athlete-specific performance research is limited and that sports medicine providers should be familiar with these devices.
paper.tldr: ENDS appear to affect the heart and lungs less than cigarettes, but the effects are not harmless and the long-term consequences are unknown. Athletes who vape may face cardiovascular, respiratory, sleep and recovery risks, and the authors suggest discouraging use, especially in athletes at higher arrhythmia risk.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on ENDS prevalence and on cardiovascular, pulmonary, sleep, injury-healing and performance effects in athletes, plus vaping-associated lung injury. The text does not describe a systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: About 47 million US adults (19.3%) use some tobacco or nicotine product, including nearly 7 million ENDS users. Nicotine from ENDS produces acute increases in blood pressure and heart rate, and habitual users show heart rate variability patterns similar to tobacco smokers. Short-term ENDS use was not shown to affect diastolic function in non-athletes, and daily male ENDS users had lower FEV1 than controls. The authors describe VALI with mostly pulmonary symptoms and with THC-containing products involved in most cases, and state that the cause is unclear.
paper.limitations: As a narrative review with no stated search method, the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Athlete-specific data are sparse, most athlete performance research is for nicotine rather than ENDS, and the authors say the cause of VALI is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports medicine providers and coaches should be able to recognise ENDS use and discuss nicotine dependence, explosion and burn risk, and VALI with athletes who vape. The authors suggest discouraging ENDS use more strongly in athletes at higher arrhythmia risk. Staff should not assume that ENDS are a safe option compared with cigarettes for athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The review offers little evidence on performance, so ENDS should not be treated as a performance aid. The authors note that the timing of nicotine use may matter for ergogenic or ergolytic effects, and that research on specific sports and events is needed.
paper.rtp: The review says ENDS use can impair sleep quality, and that nicotine may delay tendon and fracture healing, but the healing findings are largely from preclinical and tobacco studies rather than ENDS. It gives no return-to-sport criteria or timelines and cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to sport. It supports asking about ENDS use during rehabilitation.
